This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Labor, who states that in view of the fact that Mrs. Munford has already passed a civil-service examina- tion and the further fact that she has had extensive experience in the Government $e ie Department of Labor could utilize to advantage the services of Mrs. unford.

August 6, 1913. Mr. Thomas H. Vanderford may be reinstated to an appropriate position in the Internal Revenue Service without reference to the period of his separation from the service. Mr. Vanderford was a deputy collector of internal revenue from October 11, 1893, to July 10, 1898, when he was removed for political reasons. A former collector of internal revenue, under whom he served and by whom he was separated from the service, makes the following statement regarding him in a letter dated May 9, 1913: “Mr. Vanderford was an officer in the service when I was appointed collector in 1898 and had been for four years prior to my appointment. He served under me for practically a year. I regarded him as one of the best officers in the service and after 10 years’ experience as collector I think I can truthfully say he was as good an officer as I ever knew. I separated him from the service in order to appoint a man of my own party.” The Commissioner of Internal Revenue in a letter dated July 7, 1913, states that he has personally “known Mr. Vanderford for many years, that he is a man of sterling integrity, honest and fearless, and in his opinion possesses just such traits of character as would make a competent and efficient revenue officer. The records of the Internal Bevoune Bureau show that he rendered satisfactory service and was an efficient employee. In view of the above facts the commission concurs with the recommendation of the Sag of the Treasury and the Commissioner of Internal Revenue for the issuance of this order.

March 6, 1916. Mr. Carl G. Lines may be appointed as electrician at $1,200 per annum in the Bureau of the Census, Department of Commerce, without reference to the civil-service rules. Mr. Lines was appointed as electrician at $4 per diem in the Bureau of the Census on March 2, 1910, and served until January 10, 1912, under the provisions of the Executive order of December 29, 1909. He was reappointed April 23, 1914, by certification for temporary appointment by the Civil Service Commission and has served continuously since that date. In addition to performing the duties of an electrician in connection with the bureau’s machines, Mr. Lines has frequently been called upon to perform the work of a general mechanic, and his services in both respects have been highly satisfactory. This order. is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce, who states that in view of the valuable experience and training which has been acquired by ‘Mr. Lines during his temporary employment in the bureau he feels that an exception to the usual procedure is justified and ad- visable. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation.

June 26, 1916. Miss Lillian Rogenmoser, temporarily employed in the Department of State, may be appointed to a permanent nonclerical position therein, in accordance with Executive order No. 2383, of May 18, 1916, notwithstanding a lack of continuous service of six months immediately preceding July 1, 1916. Miss Rogenmoser was not eligible for permanent appointment under the order of May 18, 1916. It was stated that she was the most adaptable to the work of assisting in the printing of passports of any helper the lithographer of the department had employed during the last 10 years. Her duties were described to be the wetting down of passports to exactly the right degree and the right temperature preparatory to the printing or lithographing, and the making of records to correspond with those of the Treasury Department.

February 10, 1916. Mrs. Ethel Robards may be appointed to a clerical position in the Navy De- partment without regard to the requirement of examination under the ecivil- service rules. Mrs. Robards is the widow of Capt. Frank F. Robards, United States Marine Corps, who was killed on December 16, 1915, in the line of duty at Port au Prince, Haiti, by his horse stumbling and throwing him violently to the ground. Capt. Robards served throughout the Spanish-Ameri- can War in the Second Texas Volunteer Infantry. He was appointed second lieutenant in the United States Marine Corps July 23, 1900; promoted to first lieutenant March 3, 1903, and to captain May 13, 1908. By his death Mrs. Robards was left with a child 6 years old and without means of support except her widow’s pension of $20 a month. In view of the fact that Capt. Robards lost his life while on foreign service and in the line of duty, the commission concurs with the Secretary of the Navy in recommending an Executive order to permit her appointment. 62924°—16——8

November 9, 1914. Mr. William W. Lemmond may be transferred after reinstatement in the Depart- ment of Justice to the position of law clerk at $2,400 per annum in the office of the Judge Advocate General, War Department, without reference to the requirement of six months’ service immediately preceding transfer. Mr. Lemmond was a clerk in the classified service of the War Department from December 12, 1903, to February 25, 1907, when he was transferred to the Attorney General's Office. May 16, 1911, he was promoted to the position of assistant attorney, which he held until August 31, 1914, when he resigned. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of War, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission, in view of the statement of the Judge Advocate General that he believes Mr. Lemmond to be especially qualified for the position of law clerk by reason of his education, training, and experience in legal work in the- Department of Justice.

February 9, 1916. Mr. Edward H. Dyer, of Washington, D. C., may be appointed to a position in the Division of Efficiency, United States Civil Service Commission, with- out reference to the civil-service rules. Mr. Dyer was employed as an ac- countant by the Division of Efficiency in the work of developing and install- ing a simplified system of accounting in the Treasurer’s Office, Treasury De- partment, and had charge of the general books until they were turned over to the regular employees. He rendered valuable service in connection with said work, and his appointment to a permanent position in the Division of Effi- ciency is recommended by the chief of the division, who states that almost every piece of work which the division undertakes involves some phase of accounting for which Mr. Dyer is especially qualified.

August 2, 1916. The year limit upon eligibility for reinstatement is hereby waived to permit the reinstatement of Ernest Szemelenyi as a clerk at $1,200 per annum in the Patent Office. Mr. Szemelenyi served from 1881 to 1909 as a translator in the Patent Office. The Commissioner of Patents, who has been personally cogni- zant of the character of his work for 20 years, states that his acquaintance with foreign languages and the practical arts and science combined gives him a range of ability for handling certain business of the Patent Office which is unique; that no one has ever been able to distribute foreign patents among the different divisions as acceptably as Mr. Szemelenyi did while he was so employed ; and that he desires to have the appointment authorized by Execu- tive order because of the needs of the office and because it is impossible to get anyone to do the work which Mr. Szemelenyi can do within the salary which the office can pay. The Civil Service Commission concurs with the Secretary of the Interior in recommending this Executive order.

July 14, 1916. Miss Ruth L. O'Donnell may be appointed to a position in the Bureau of Effi- ciency without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Chief of the Bureau of Efficiency, who states that Miss O’Donnell has been employed in his office at various times during the past two years; that her services have been most satisfactory; and that her permanent appointment to the force of the Bureau of Efficiency would be a distinct advan- tage to the bureau. October 1, 1914. Mrs. Fannie L. Hopkins, of Virginia, who is now on the civil-service eligible list for appointment as a clerk, may be appointed a clerk at $1,000 per annum in the Department of State, upon the retirement of her mother, Mrs. Mary D. May 11, 1915. Miss Agnes Deery may be appointed as a nurse in the Indian Service without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. . Sweet may be appointed to a clerical position on the per- manent roll of the Treasury Department without compliance with the require- ments of the civil-service rules. Mr. George Tumlin, of Decatur, Ga., may be appointed as superintendent of the farm and transportation at the Atlanta Penitentiary without regard to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. In the opinion of the Postmaster General Mr. Inch is thoroughly quali- fied for the position. The Civil Service Commission ‘does not concur in the recommendation for the issuance of this order.

December 14, 1915. Miss Emma I. Windridge, who has passed the civil-service examination in stenography and typewriting, may be appointed to a clerkship in the War Department without reference to the civil-service rules. Miss Windridge is the daughter of Charles E. Windridge, formerly a clerk in the War Department. Her father was appointed to a position in the Post Office Department in Novem- ber, 1902, where he served until April, 1905, when he was appointed -to a posi- tion in the Navy Department. He resigned in November, 1905, to accept a clerk- ship in the War Department, which he held until the time of his death, Sep- tember 14, 1915. Mr. Windridge had an excellent record while employed in the ‘War Department. The Secretary of War recommends the issuance of an order in this case. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommen- dation.

June 26, 1915. Mr. Edward E. Carter may be reinstated in the Forest Service as forest inspector at $2,800 per annum without regard to the year limit of the reinstatement rule. Mr. Carter entered the Forest Service through the field assistant in forestry exami- nation on March 11,1905, and resigned on September 30,1910. Hissalary wasincreased from $1,000 to $2,500 per annum by successive promotions from forest assistant to forest inspector, chief of office of management, and assistant forester. His duties during the last two and one-half years of that period were identical with those which will now be required, namely, the administration and field inspection of timber sales, timber reconnaissance, and reforestation. His exceptional capacity had placed himg in rank next to the assistant forester in charge of the branch of silviculture, and in the absence of that officer he handled the entire executive work of the branch. From 1910 to the present time Mr. Carter has been employed continuously as assistant professor in forestry at Harvard University, specializing on forest management, silviculture and the administration of the forest property of the university. This experience and training are regarded by the department as an added qualification for the special duties of the existing vacancy. The department regards Mr. Carter as one of the strongest men in technical forestry ever employed by the Forest Service. In view of these facts the commission concurs with the department in recommend- ing this order.
